concerns.text: FR-003 defines the target variable ('first arrival') as the week where cumulative count exceeds 5% of the ANNUAL TOTAL. This creates a circular dependency: the target for a specific year is determined by the total count of that same year. If a year has low detection (low total), the 5% threshold is reached earlier in the season (or never), conflating 'migration timing' with 'detection effort'. The target is not independent of the observation process, violating the independence of validation targets from predictors.

US-3 and FR-006 propose using a paired t-test to compare RMSE/correlation of models. However, the 'first arrival' metric is a derived scalar per grid-cell/year. If the dataset consists of N grid cells, the t-test assumes N independent samples. Migration events in adjacent grid cells are spatially autocorrelated (not independent). Using a standard t-test on spatially clustered data violates the independence assumption of the statistical test, leading to inflated Type I error rates (false positives).

The spec proposes a temporal split (2015-2020 train, 2022 test) for a spatially distributed phenomenon. While this prevents temporal leakage, it fails to address spatial generalization. A model trained on 2015-2020 data may learn region-specific biases. The validation strategy does not explicitly require a spatial hold-out (e.g., training on East Coast, testing on West Coast) to prove the model captures general migration drivers rather than local site effects.

FR-003 lists the sensitivity sweep set as '{[deferred], [deferred], [deferred]}'. While placeholders are allowed, the set should explicitly include the baseline (5%) and at least one alternative (e.g., 3% or 10%) to demonstrate the *intent* of the sensitivity analysis, rather than leaving all slots as deferred. This obscures the experimental design.
